zin: What if you were William of Orange?
At eleven, you'd inherit a fortune and a whole principality.
You'd stand at the side of the most powerful man on earth.
Then you'd give it all up, to fight his son.
And you'd become one of the first leaders in history to be killed with a pistol.
So how does the richest nobleman in the Netherlands end up starting a war that lasts eighty years?
You're born in 1533, in a castle called Dillenburg, in the middle of Germany.
Your father is a count, but not a rich one.
You're the oldest of twelve children, and the house is loud.
Your family is Lutheran, and you grow up with Bible lessons at the table.
Then, in 1544, a cousin you barely know is killed in a siege in France.
He has no children, and in his will, he leaves everything to you.
The little principality of Orange, in the south of France.
And huge estates all over the Netherlands.
At eleven, you're suddenly a prince, and one of the richest people in Europe.
But there's a catch.
The emperor, Charles the Fifth, only agrees if you're raised a Catholic, at his court in Brussels.
So you say goodbye to your parents, and you leave.
In Brussels, you learn French, Spanish, fencing and dancing.
You learn to ride, to hunt, and to keep your thoughts to yourself.
And Charles the Fifth starts to like you.
He rules Spain, half of Italy, the Netherlands, and a new empire in America.
It's said the sun never sets on his lands.
At eighteen, you marry Anna of Egmond, one of the richest girls in the country.
You throw huge parties, and you spend money like water.
At twenty-one, the emperor puts you in charge of an army.
Then, in 1555, the old emperor is tired and sick.
In a great hall in Brussels, he gives up his throne.
And as he walks in, he leans on one shoulder for support.
Your shoulder.
The new ruler of the Netherlands is his son, Philip the Second.
And Philip doesn't like you at all.
In 1559, you're sent to France, as a hostage for a peace treaty.
One day, you go hunting with the French king, Henry the Second.
He thinks you're in on Philip's plans, so he tells you a secret.
Together, the two kings want to root out every Protestant in their lands.
You think of your parents, and your brothers and sisters.
But you say nothing.
That's what you yourself would later write, and the legend gave you a nickname: William the Silent.
Back home, Philip makes you governor of Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht.
Then he sails to Spain, and never comes back.
From far away, he sends orders: hunt down the heretics.
People are burned for owning the wrong book.
And in 1564, in front of the whole council, you say it out loud.
A king, you say, has no right to rule over the consciences of his people.
In 1566, hundreds of nobles march into the palace with a petition.
An adviser sneers that they're nothing but beggars.
So they turn it into their name, and start wearing beggar's bowls around their necks.
That summer, angry crowds storm the churches and smash the statues.
In Madrid, Philip is furious.
He sends his hardest general, the Duke of Alba, with about ten thousand veteran soldiers.
You see it coming, and you flee to Germany before he arrives.
Your friends, the counts of Egmont and Horn, decide to stay.
Alba sets up a court the people call the Council of Blood.
More than a thousand people are executed, among them Egmont and Horn.
Your lands are taken.
And your oldest son, thirteen years old, is taken from his university and shipped to Spain.
You will never see him again.
So you do something no one expects from the emperor's old favourite.
You sell your silver, your jewels, everything you have, and you raise an army.
In 1568, your brothers win the first battle, at Heiligerlee.
But your brother Adolf dies in the fighting.
Your own army marches into the south, waiting for the cities to rise up.
They don't.
Alba refuses to fight, and simply follows you until your money runs out.
Your soldiers go home, unpaid, and you're broke.
Then, help comes from the sea.
The Sea Beggars, rebel pirates sailing in your name, take the port of Brill.
It's the first of April, 1572.
Brill means glasses in Dutch, so people joke: on April Fools' Day, Alba lost his glasses.
One city after another opens its gates to the rebels.
And around this time, someone writes a song about you.
The first letters of its verses spell your name, William of Nassau.
It's called the Wilhelmus, and today it's the Dutch national anthem.
But in the south, everything goes wrong.
In Paris, thousands of Protestants are murdered in a single night, and your French allies are gone.
You go to Holland, and write that you'll make your grave there.
In 1573, you officially become a Calvinist.
A year later, your brothers Louis and Henry are killed in a battle on the heath of Mook.
Now three of your brothers have died in this war.
Meanwhile, the Spanish surround the city of Leiden.
Inside, people are eating rats, and dying of hunger and plague.
So you make a terrible choice.
You order the dikes to be cut, and you flood your own land.
Farms and fields disappear under the water.
Your fleet sails over the meadows, right up to the walls of the city.
The Spanish flee, and the starving people of Leiden get herring and white bread.
As a reward, you give the city a university, the first one in the north.
In 1579, the northern provinces sign the Union of Utrecht, and promise to fight together.
Philip has had enough.
In 1580, he declares you an outlaw, an enemy of the human race.
Anyone who kills you will get twenty-five thousand gold crowns, and a title.
You answer with a long letter to every court in Europe.
In it, you call the king a liar and a murderer.
A year later, the rebel provinces go even further.
They declare that a king who oppresses his people is no longer their king.
Some historians see it as one of the models for the American Declaration of Independence, two centuries later.
In March 1582, in Antwerp, a young man walks up to you after dinner.
He fires a pistol, right into your face.
The bullet goes through your cheek and your jaw, and you survive.
Your third wife, Charlotte, nurses you day and night.
You get better, but she is exhausted, and she dies a few weeks later.
Two years later, you're living in Delft, in an old convent called the Prinsenhof.
A quiet young man has been visiting you, pretending to be a Protestant refugee.
His name is Balthasar Gérard, and he wants the reward.
On the tenth of July, 1584, you walk out of the dining room.
He's waiting at the foot of the stairs.
This time, he doesn't miss.
According to tradition, your last words are: my God, have pity on my soul, and on this poor people.
The bullet holes are still in the wall today.
You die at fifty-one, deep in debt, because you spent your whole fortune on the war.
The war goes on for sixty-four more years.
In 1648, Spain finally recognises the Dutch Republic as a free country.
The Dutch call you the Father of the Fatherland.
Your family still sits on the Dutch throne, as the House of Orange.
And on the king's birthday, the whole country dresses in orange.
There's even a story that Dutch farmers bred orange carrots in your honour, but that one is probably a myth.
Not bad, for the boy from Dillenburg who said nothing.
Who should be born next? Tell us in the comments.
